```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = '#>', fig.width = 9,
                     fig.height = 4, out.width = '100%')
library(grip)
recipe <- system.file('scripts', 'metric-mds-comparison.R', package = 'grip')
source(recipe, local = TRUE)
bundle <- readRDS(system.file('extdata', 'metric-mds-comparison', 'benchmark.rds', package = 'grip'))
rows <- comparison_rows(bundle)
last <- rows[rows$budget == 100L & rows$status == 'ok', ]
paired <- merge(last[last$backend == 'sgd', c('case','seed','error')],
                last[last$backend == 'smacof', c('case','seed','error')],
                by = c('case','seed'), suffixes = c('.sgd','.smacof'))
have.ivue <- isTRUE(getOption('grip.vignette.interactive', TRUE)) &&
  requireNamespace('ivue', quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace('rgl', quietly = TRUE) &&
  all(c('plot3D.groups','color.scale.groups','layer3D.mesh','layer3D.edges','layer3D.axes','camera.zup') %in% getNamespaceExports('ivue')) &&
  'limits' %in% names(formals(ivue::plot3D.plain))
```

## What is being compared?

`metric.mds()` fits Euclidean coordinates to graph shortest-path distances.
Its default `backend = "sgd"` uses native stochastic gradient descent (SGD),
based on [Zheng, Pawar and Goodman (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2018.2859997),
with the default learning-rate schedule following
[Hangan, Kobourov and Miller (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00641).
SGD visits pairs of points in a randomly shuffled order, moving each pair
closer together or farther apart to better match its target distance. These
changes take effect immediately, and the learning-rate schedule reduces the
size of the adjustments as fitting proceeds.

The alternative `backend = "smacof"` uses the optional **smacof** package
([Mair, Groenen and de Leeuw, 2022](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v102.i10)).
SMACOF combines information from all pairs before updating the entire
configuration at once. Each update is designed to reduce total stress;
an individual SGD adjustment need not reduce total stress, even though it
improves the distance for the pair being adjusted.
With the default `pair.weights = "uniform"`, both minimize the same raw distance stress:

\[
S(Z) = \sum_{i<j} \bigl(\lVert z_i-z_j\rVert-d_{ij}\bigr)^2.
\]

Both also support `pair.weights = "inverse_squared"`, the graph-drawing
weighting used by [Zheng, Pawar and Goodman (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2018.2859997).
The [weighting comparison](#the-effect-of-stress-weighting) below shows how
this changes the fitted layouts. The original 420-fit comparison uses uniform
weighting throughout.

This is a comparison of these implementations and settings on small synthetic
examples. For a more extensive comparison of SGD and SMACOF across 18 benchmark
datasets, see [Hangan, Kobourov and Miller (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00641),
who compare their SGD solver with scikit-learn's SMACOF implementation.

The figure labels and plots use **normalized error**,
\(\sqrt{S(Z)/\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}^2}\). Lower is better; zero means exact agreement
with the target distances. Within a dataset, its ranking is identical to raw
stress. Raw stress is also reported. We recompute both from the returned
coordinates, rather than compare differently normalized backend reports.

The precomputed experiment uses 14 datasets, five paired starts, three
allowances, and two backends: **420 planned fits**. Every example is displayed
below, including both cloud sizes. Except for the planar control, all fits
and interactive views are three-dimensional. The plane is fitted and plotted
in two dimensions.

## A small, executable example

Construct a saddle over \([-1,1]^2\), with
\(z=0.8(x^2-y^2)\). This is a two-dimensional surface embedded in 3D.
To compare ambient distances, represent the cloud as a complete graph with
Euclidean edge lengths. The triangle inequality then makes graph shortest-path
distances equal to the original Euclidean distances.

```{r saddle-example}
library(grip)
source(system.file('scripts', 'metric-mds-comparison.R', package = 'grip'), local = TRUE)
grid <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 5)
uv <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x = grid, y = grid))
X <- cbind(uv, z = .8 * (uv[, 1]^2 - uv[, 2]^2))
edges <- t(combn(nrow(X), 2))
lengths <- sqrt(rowSums((X[edges[, 1], ] - X[edges[, 2], ])^2))
prepared <- prepare.graph.geodesic.mds(edges = edges, n = nrow(X),
                                      edge.weights = lengths)
start <- withr::with_seed(11, matrix(rnorm(nrow(X) * 3), nrow(X), 3))
# Schedule completion emits an iteration-limit warning, not convergence.
sgd <- suppressWarnings(metric.mds(prepared = prepared, dim = 3,
  init = start, n.init = 1, max.iter = 30, seed = 11, diagnostics = FALSE))
sgd$metadata$engine  # "sgd": backend omitted deliberately
sgd$metadata$termination
smacof.fit <- NULL
if (requireNamespace('smacof', quietly = TRUE)) {
  smacof.fit <- suppressWarnings(metric.mds(prepared = prepared, dim = 3,
    init = start, n.init = 1, max.iter = 30, seed = 11,
    backend = 'smacof', eps = 1e-8, diagnostics = FALSE))
  rbind(SGD = comparison_score(sgd$coords, prepared$distance_matrix),
        SMACOF = comparison_score(smacof.fit$coords, prepared$distance_matrix))
}
```

This introductory 25-point fit is separate from the timing experiment.
Its coordinates are also shown: the timing labels below belong only to the
saved experiment, not to this run during document generation.

```{r small-example-view, fig.cap="The executable 25-point saddle example: gray reference, blue SGD, orange SMACOF (when available). Both fits use the same starting coordinates and 30 passes/iterations."}
small.case <- comparison_cases(5L)[['saddle-25']]
small.fits <- list(sgd = list(coords = sgd$coords),
  smacof = list(coords = if (!is.null(smacof.fit)) smacof.fit$coords else NULL))
if (have.ivue) {
  comparison_view(small.case, small.fits)
} else {
  # A 3D projection of this run; precomputed experiment images below use ivue.
  Z <- cbind(small.case$X[,1], small.case$X[,2], small.case$X[,3])
  Zs <- comparison_align(sgd$coords, Z)
  view <- function(A) cbind(.8*A[,1] - .6*A[,2], .3*A[,1] + .4*A[,2] + .866*A[,3])
  all <- rbind(Z, Zs)
  colors <- rep(c('gray55','#1769AA'), each = nrow(Z))
  if (!is.null(small.fits$smacof$coords)) {
    all <- rbind(all, comparison_align(small.fits$smacof$coords, Z))
    colors <- c(colors, rep('#D66A19', nrow(Z)))
  }
  plot(view(all), asp = 1, pch = 16, col = colors,
       xlab = '3D projection: horizontal', ylab = '3D projection: vertical')
}
```

`max.iter` defaults to 1000; 30 is an explicit short trial allowance.
One SGD pass visits all unordered pairs. One SMACOF iteration is a different
operation, so equal iteration counts are not equal work. SGD's schedule ends
with `iteration_limit`, even when it returns an earlier, better checkpoint.
SMACOF may stop earlier using `eps`; this tolerance must not be passed to SGD.
The learning-rate defaults are provisional calibration choices.

## Datasets and timing protocol

The plane, paraboloid and saddle use regular 8-by-8 and 12-by-12 grids on
\([-1,1]^2\), giving 64 and 144 vertices. Their lifts are, respectively,
\(z=0\), \(z=0.8(x^2+y^2)\), and \(z=0.8(x^2-y^2)\).
The Gaussian clouds have three independent standard-normal coordinates with
fixed seeds. The spatial graph follows a helix
\((\cos t,\sin t,t/\pi)\), \(0\leq t\leq3\pi\), with edges between consecutive
vertices and between vertices seven indices apart. Every graph edge is
weighted by its Euclidean length in the generating coordinates.

For the paraboloid and saddle, two target definitions are compared:

- **Ambient Euclidean:** all straight-line distances in the generating 3D
  cloud, represented by a complete weighted graph. An exact 3D realization
  exists; classical MDS provides a useful numerical check.
- **Local graph paths:** shortest paths on the grid with horizontal, vertical,
  and both diagonal connections. These are exact distances for that finite
  graph, **not exact geodesic distances on the continuous quadform**. They
  depend on sampling and allowed directions. Small graph-distance stress need
  not reconstruct the generating surface.

The helix uses local graph-path targets. Its generating coordinates are a
reference drawing, not a guaranteed exact realization of all graph distances.
The reference mesh on each quadform connects corresponding sampled vertices;
it is a display aid, not a geodesic or surface-recovery certificate.

For every dataset, both backends receive the **same saved starting-coordinate
recipe**, for seeds 1–5, and `n.init = 1`. Each allowance of 10, 30 or 100
starts a separate fit from those coordinates. SGD uses the hybrid schedule
with initial rate 0.5, boundary rate 0.01, switch fraction 0.4, and scoring after
every pass; SMACOF uses `eps = 1e-8`. Backend order alternates between paired
blocks. No setting was chosen from the observed winners.

Elapsed fitting time includes the wrapper, target normalization, optimization,
and checkpoint scoring. Shared graph preparation, process startup, namespace
loading, independent final scoring, alignment, and rendering are excluded.
The two namespaces are loaded before timing either backend. Each fit runs in
an isolated process with a 30-second allowance; the full experiment has a
1,800-second allowance. Errors and timeouts remain in the result table and
are not replaced by successful reruns. These are provisional workload limits.

The plots show median time and median normalized error across five starts,
with horizontal and vertical interquartile ranges. Numeric labels identify
the allowances. **Each marker is a separate restarted experiment, not a
checkpoint on one optimization trajectory.** There is no retrospective
best-of-three selection. Values below 0.001 seconds or error below \(10^{-12}\)
are clipped only for logarithmic plotting; the tables retain measured values.

```{r run-status}
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(Backend = rows$backend, Status = rows$status)),
             col.names = c('Backend','Outcome','Fits'))
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(split(rows, rows$backend), function(z) {
  data.frame(Backend = z$backend[1], Fits = nrow(z),
    `Successful fits` = sum(z$status == 'ok'),
    `Total fit seconds` = sum(z$seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Total worker seconds` = sum(z$worker_seconds), check.names = FALSE)
})), row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
```

At the largest allowance (100 passes/iterations), SGD has lower normalized
error in **`r sum(paired$error.sgd < paired$error.smacof - 1e-10)` of
`r nrow(paired)` completed pairs**, and SMACOF in
**`r sum(paired$error.smacof < paired$error.sgd - 1e-10)`**; differences no larger
than \(10^{-10}\) count as ties. This compares a specified iteration allowance,
not equal elapsed time. Across all three allowances, total recorded fitting
time is **`r sprintf('%.3f', sum(rows$seconds[rows$backend == 'sgd'], na.rm = TRUE))`
seconds for SGD** and **`r sprintf('%.3f', sum(rows$seconds[rows$backend == 'smacof'], na.rm = TRUE))`
for SMACOF**. These examples favor SGD's achieved accuracy but do not establish
a universal speed advantage. Use the per-example plots to examine the trade-off.

An `ok` outcome means a fit returned usable coordinates; it does not mean
convergence. Figure tables below report the actual pass/iteration count and
termination reason. Worker time includes startup and communication and is
reported separately.
For a forcibly stopped worker, fitting time may be unavailable; summing
recorded fitting time alone would then understate total effort.
Timing is machine-dependent, especially for these small examples. This run
used a shared workstation without CPU isolation; short timings are sensitive
to background activity and timer resolution.

## How to read the embedding figures

**Gray is the generating reference; blue is SGD; orange is SMACOF.** Each
saved experiment figure shows seed 1 and allowance 100, selected in advance
and identically for both backends. It is not the best seed or the fit nearest
the median. A failed selected run stays unavailable. Figure tables report
that exact run's error, raw stress and fitting time, as well as a separately
computed classical-MDS reference.

For overlays we center each fit, then apply an orthogonal rotation/reflection
to match corresponding reference vertices. **No rescaling is performed for
alignment.** The reported scores use original returned coordinates. These
operations preserve all fitted distances; shared axes retain the input units.
Blue and orange graph segments show the same edges in each embedding. Dense
complete graphs are shown as clouds, avoiding thousands of overlapping edges.

Side-by-side panels first show the reference and each backend separately, with
common limits, camera and scale. The overlay below them shows their agreement.
With a current `ivue` (including mesh layers and shared view limits) and `rgl`
available, drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. Otherwise,
the figures use saved images of these same `ivue` views. The plane uses 2D
panels. To inspect just one configuration, recreate a view with `show` set to
`"reference"`, `"sgd"`, or `"smacof"`:

```{r individual-view, eval=FALSE}
bundle <- readRDS(system.file('extdata', 'metric-mds-comparison',
                              'benchmark.rds', package = 'grip'))
case <- bundle$cases[['saddle_graph-144']]
fits <- comparison_representative(bundle, case$id)
comparison_view(case, fits, show = 'sgd')
comparison_view(case, fits, show = 'smacof')
comparison_view(case, fits, show = 'overlay')
```

`ivue` is optional and is available from
[its source repository](https://github.com/pgajer/ivue). Its public
`plot3D.groups()`, `layer3D.mesh()`, `layer3D.edges()`, `layer3D.axes()`
and `camera.zup()` methods
build these views. It does not fit or modify the embeddings. Set
`options(grip.vignette.interactive = FALSE)` before rendering to use the saved
images even when ivue is installed. Overlapping colors may hide very close
fits; the single-method views above help inspect them separately.

```{r experiment-figures, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
kinds <- c('gaussian','plane','paraboloid','saddle','paraboloid_graph','saddle_graph','helix_graph')
for (kind in kinds) {
  ids <- paste(kind, c(64,144), sep = '-')
  case <- bundle$cases[[ids[1]]]
  cat('\n\n## ', case$label, ': ', case$target, '\n\n', sep = '')
  child <- c(
    sprintf('```{r tradeoff-%s, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Separate schedules: median normalized error versus median fitting time; bars show the interquartile ranges over five starts. Labels are pass/iteration allowances."}', kind),
    sprintf('comparison_tradeoff(bundle, c("%s", "%s"))', ids[1], ids[2]), '```')
  cat(knitr::knit_child(text = child, envir = environment(), quiet = TRUE), sep = '\n')
  for (id in ids) {
    child <- c(sprintf('### %s points', bundle$cases[[id]]$n),
      sprintf('```{r table-%s, echo=FALSE}', id),
      sprintf('case <- bundle$cases[["%s"]]', id),
      'fits <- comparison_representative(bundle, case$id)',
      'reference <- comparison_score(case$X[,seq_len(case$dimension),drop=FALSE], case$distances)',
      'classical <- bundle$baseline[[case$id]]',
      'tab <- data.frame(Method = c("Generating reference", "Classical MDS", "SGD", "SMACOF"),',
      '  Raw_stress = c(reference[["raw_stress"]], classical$score[["raw_stress"]], fits$sgd$row$raw_stress, fits$smacof$row$raw_stress),',
      '  Normalized_error = c(reference[["error"]], classical$score[["error"]], fits$sgd$row$error, fits$smacof$row$error),',
      '  Fit_seconds = c(NA, classical$seconds, fits$sgd$row$seconds, fits$smacof$row$seconds),',
      '  Iterations = c(NA, NA, fits$sgd$row$iterations, fits$smacof$row$iterations),',
      '  Termination = c("Reference only", "Spectral reference", if (fits$sgd$row$status == "ok") fits$sgd$row$termination else fits$sgd$row$status, if (fits$smacof$row$status == "ok") fits$smacof$row$termination else fits$smacof$row$status))',
      'tab$Raw_stress <- format(tab$Raw_stress, scientific = TRUE, digits = 4)',
      'tab$Normalized_error <- format(tab$Normalized_error, scientific = TRUE, digits = 4)',
      'knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3, col.names = c("Method", "Raw stress", "Normalized error", "Fit seconds", "Passes/iterations", "Termination"))', '```',
      sprintf('```{r embedding-%s, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Fixed seed 1, allowance 100. Gray: generating reference; blue: SGD; orange: SMACOF. The table above reports the exact displayed fits. Alignment preserves scale."}', id),
      'if (case$dimension != 2L) knitr::include_graphics(system.file("extdata", "metric-mds-comparison", paste0(case$id, "-panels.png"), package = "grip"))',
      '```',
      sprintf('```{r overlay-%s, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5}', id),
      'if (case$dimension == 2L) {',
      '  comparison_planar(case, fits)',
      '} else if (have.ivue) {',
      '  comparison_view(case, fits)',
      '} else {',
      '  knitr::include_graphics(system.file("extdata", "metric-mds-comparison", paste0(case$id, ".png"), package = "grip"))',
      '}', '```')
    cat(knitr::knit_child(text = child, envir = environment(), quiet = TRUE), sep = '\n')
  }
}
```

## The effect of stress weighting

Uniform stress measures squared errors in distance units. The paper's weighting
instead minimizes squared **relative** errors:

\[
S_{\mathrm{relative}}(Z)
= \sum_{i<j}\frac{(\lVert z_i-z_j\rVert-d_{ij})^2}{d_{ij}^2}.
\]

For example, an error of 0.2 on a target distance of 1 counts as much as an error
of 2 on a target distance of 10. Thus shorter distances receive more influence
than under uniform weighting. This changes the objective for both optimizers;
it is separate from the edge lengths used to compute graph shortest paths.

Select the same weighting for either backend:

```{r weighted-api, eval=FALSE}
sgd <- metric.mds(prepared = prepared, dim = 3, init = start,
                 backend = "sgd", pair.weights = "inverse_squared",
                 max.iter = 100, diagnostics = FALSE)
smacof <- metric.mds(prepared = prepared, dim = 3, init = start,
                    backend = "smacof", pair.weights = "inverse_squared",
                    max.iter = 100, eps = 1e-8, diagnostics = FALSE)
```

Set `pair.weights = "uniform"` to use the original objective. Inverse-squared
weighting requires positive distances between distinct vertices; zero distances
are rejected rather than replaced by a small constant. The learning-rate
schedule stays the same as above, in RMS-normalized distance units. These fits
use the paper's weighting, with grip's documented schedule and initialization.

This **separate 60-fit experiment** compares the saddle, paraboloid, and spatial
helix graphs with 64 vertices each. Each backend and weighting receives the same
five random starting shapes, seeds 1–5, with one start per fit and an allowance
of 100 passes or iterations. The wrapper fits the initial and final coordinate
scale to the selected objective. The allowance, SGD controls, and SMACOF
tolerance match the original comparison. Each worker has 30 seconds; the whole
experiment has 600 seconds. Failed fits remain in the results.

Every returned layout is scored under **both** definitions: uniform normalized
error and root-mean-square relative error. Compare rows within the same error
column. The two columns measure different goals; their magnitudes do not select
a universally better weighting. Reported scores use the returned coordinates
without fitting another scale for the other objective.

```{r weighting-results, include=FALSE}
weighting.bundle <- readRDS(system.file('extdata','metric-mds-weighting',
                                      'benchmark.rds',package='grip'))
weighting.rows <- comparison_rows(weighting.bundle)
weighting.summary <- comparison_summary(weighting.bundle)
weighting.pairs <- merge(
  weighting.summary[weighting.summary$pair_weights=='uniform',c('case','backend','uniform_error','relative_error')],
  weighting.summary[weighting.summary$pair_weights=='inverse_squared',c('case','backend','uniform_error','relative_error')],
  by=c('case','backend'),suffixes=c('.uniform','.inverse'))
```

The run returned coordinates for **`r sum(weighting.rows$status == 'ok')` of
`r nrow(weighting.rows)` fits**. As above, a returned fit does not imply
convergence. Tables give medians across all five starts and then the scores of
the exact displayed runs. The figures use the preselected seed 1. All four
layouts and the gray generating reference share the same camera and scale;
Procrustes alignment uses corresponding vertices without resizing.

In this run, inverse-squared weighting lowered median relative error in
**`r sum(weighting.pairs$relative_error.inverse < weighting.pairs$relative_error.uniform)`
of `r nrow(weighting.pairs)` graph–backend comparisons**, while increasing median
uniform error in **`r sum(weighting.pairs$uniform_error.inverse > weighting.pairs$uniform_error.uniform)`**.
The figures show how that change in priorities alters each layout.

```{r weighting-figures, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
for (id in names(weighting.bundle$cases)) {
  case <- weighting.bundle$cases[[id]]
  fits <- comparison_weighting_fits(weighting.bundle,id)
  cat('\n\n### ',case$label,': uniform versus inverse-squared weights\n\n',sep='')
  med <- weighting.summary[weighting.summary$case==id,]
  med$backend <- toupper(med$backend)
  med$pair_weights <- ifelse(med$pair_weights=='uniform','Uniform','Inverse-squared')
  cat('Medians across five starting shapes:\n\n')
  cat(knitr::kable(med[,c('backend','pair_weights','successful','attempted',
                         'uniform_error','relative_error','seconds')],
    row.names=FALSE,digits=4,col.names=c('Backend','Weighting','Returned','Attempted',
      'Uniform error','Relative error','Fit seconds')),sep='\n')
  shown <- do.call(rbind,lapply(fits,`[[`,'row'))
  shown$backend <- toupper(shown$backend)
  shown$pair_weights <- ifelse(shown$pair_weights=='uniform','Uniform','Inverse-squared')
  cat('\n\nDisplayed runs (seed 1):\n\n')
  cat(knitr::kable(shown[,c('backend','pair_weights','uniform_error','relative_error',
                          'seconds','termination','status')], row.names=FALSE,digits=4,
    col.names=c('Backend','Weighting','Uniform error','Relative error','Fit seconds','Termination','Status')),sep='\n')
  child <- c(
    sprintf('```{r weighting-panels-%s, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Each panel shows one fitted layout against the gray generating reference. The interactive view below combines all four layouts; its legend identifies each backend and weighting."}',id),
    sprintf('knitr::include_graphics(system.file("extdata","metric-mds-weighting","%s-panels.png",package="grip"))',id),'```',
    sprintf('```{r weighting-overlay-%s, echo=FALSE}',id),
    'if (have.ivue) { comparison_view(case,fits,weighting=TRUE) } else {',
    sprintf('knitr::include_graphics(system.file("extdata","metric-mds-weighting","%s.png",package="grip"))',id),'}','```')
  cat(knitr::knit_child(text=child,envir=environment(),quiet=TRUE),sep='\n')
}
```

## Sparse SGD for larger graphs

`metric.mds(approximation = "sparse")` uses representative vertices (pivots) to approximate
long-range interactions while retaining graph edges. It implements the sparse
SGD method of [Zheng et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2018.2859997),
based on [Ortmann et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.7155/jgaa.00440), with
inverse-squared weighting and no all-pairs distance preparation.

See [Sparse SGD for larger graphs](sparse-metric-mds.html) for usage and a
separate comparison of full SGD, sparse SGD with several pivot counts, and
weighted GRIP. It includes 3D views, repeated runs, total layout times, measured
peak memory, and an independently scored 4,096-vertex saddle.

## Reproduce the experiment

Building this vignette runs the small example and displays saved results for
the larger comparison. To repeat all 420 fits, install the R packages **callr**
and **smacof**, then run these commands in the grip source folder:

```sh
mkdir -p ../comparison-library
R CMD INSTALL --preclean --library=../comparison-library . > ../comparison-install.log 2>&1
Rscript tools/pkg/build-metric-mds-comparison.R ../fresh-results ../comparison-library ../comparison-install.log
```

To repeat the separate weighting comparison, add `weighting` as the final
argument and choose another results folder:

```sh
Rscript tools/pkg/build-metric-mds-comparison.R ../fresh-weighting-results ../comparison-library ../comparison-install.log weighting
```

The script saves the timings, fitted coordinates, and any errors in
`fresh-results`, beside the grip source folder. Choose a new results folder
for each run. Instructions for
recreating the figures are in the
[reproduction guide](https://github.com/pgajer/grip/blob/main/tools/README.md#metric-mds-comparison-vignette).

- Hangan, D., Kobourov, S. and Miller, J. (2026).
  *Bridging Graph Drawing and Dimensionality Reduction with Stochastic Stress
  Optimization*. [arXiv:2605.00641](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00641).

- Mair, P., Groenen, P. J. F. and de Leeuw, J. (2022).
  *More on Multidimensional Scaling and Unfolding in R: smacof Version 2*.
  Journal of Statistical Software, 102(10).
  [doi:10.18637/jss.v102.i10](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v102.i10).
